transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
The Trump administration's Justice Department has made a highly unusual court filing about
the U.S. Senate race in Alaska, and PR's Hansi Lo Wang reports the filing asks a federal
judge to block the certification of the election results if the Republican incumbent loses.
Out of the four U.S. Senate candidates in Alaska, two have similar names, the sitting
senator Dan Sullivan, a Republican, and Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., who is not affiliated with
a local party.
Alaska's Republican Party supported an earlier lawsuit in state court that tried to stop
this, but in June, the Alaska Supreme Court ruled that Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. has the
right to run as a candidate.
Now in a federal court filing, the Justice Department says that if Republican Senator
Dan Sullivan does not win, a judge should block Alaska from certifying the election
results.
The DOJ argues those results could be "impacted by voter confusion."
Many election law experts are skeptical of the Justice Department's argument, which
cites the preamble of the National Voter Registration Act.
Hansi Lo Wang, NPR News.
Ukraine says its military is still encountering disruptions with Star Shield, the military
version of Starlink technology critical to Ukraine's drone-related war effort against
Russia.
Yesterday, The Wall Street Journal reported President Trump called SpaceX chief Elon Musk
and asked him to lift restrictions.
The Wall Street Journal's National Security reporter Alex Ward spoke to NPR's Here and
Now.
You had President Trump call Elon Musk and say, "Hey, we see that the speeds of this
Star Shield S subscription are still capped at 160 kilometers an hour, about 100 miles
per hour, and I want those raised."
And Trump left that conversation believing they were going to go up.
Within a couple of hours, it became clear that the Ukrainians were getting at somewhat
higher speeds, but that only lasted a small amount of time and in certain spaces.
So as of right now, it still seems to be slowed down and that's impacting the war.
And even President Trump, speaking to reporters today, said, "If it is still down, I'll have
to talk to Elon again."
The administration has decided to abandon its efforts to tighten the rules around a popular
student loan forgiveness program.
More from NPR's Corey Turner.
Public service loan forgiveness was created by Congress as a way to encourage college
grads to work in lower paying public service and nonprofit jobs.
And in return, after 10 years, they'd have their loans forgiven.
But last year, the administration attempted to create a new rule that any employer with
"substantial, illegal purpose" could be disqualified along with its employees.
The Education Department was vague, though, on what exactly those three words mean.
And a combination of states and nonprofits sued, arguing the administration could use
that vagueness to punish any group, even a city or state employer, that doesn't share
its politics.
A pair of recent court rulings agreed, and this week the Justice Department dropped its
appeal.
Corey Turner, NPR News.
This is NPR.
Prince Harry's wife, Meghan, says she is deeply distressed by allegations that images of child
sexual abuse were found at her father's former home in the Philippines.
She says her thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed.
The Duchess of Sussex issued her statement today in response to a report in the British
tabloid newspaper The Sun.
It reported that her brother found the pictures while clearing out Thomas Markle Sr.'s home.
The Daily Mail reported that the 82-year-old Markle, who returned to the United States,
denied the allegations.
The editor-in-chief of one of Egypt's most widely recognized independent news websites
has been charged with operating an unlicensed media outlet.
NPR's Eba Trawi reports this comes as part of a larger suppression of press freedoms
in Egypt.
The independent English and Arabic news outlet Meda Masra says its editor-in-chief Lina Atalla
is being charged with establishing, managing and operating a website without a license.
The Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights says Atalla will be tried by state prosecutors
after she was released on bail Thursday following more than six hours of questioning.
Meda Masra says it legally challenged the state's rejection of its request for a license
in 2022 and that its request for a license has been pending since 2023.
Atalla is the recipient of multiple international journalism awards.
Amnesty International says her case reflects a wider crackdown following the arrest this
month of six journalists from the Egyptian fact-checking website Matzadeh Dash.
Eba Trawi, NPR News, Dubai.
This is NPR News.

Ukraine says Starlink military version Star Shield still disrupted despite Trump's call to Musk
Trump administration drops appeal over Public Service Loan Forgiveness employer eligibility rule
